Menelaus

GeometryTrianglesFractions
Game: Move dots on a triangle to see when three lines meet in one place and when three dots fall on one straight line.
How to play: Drag a dot, or focus it and use the arrow keys. Press Ceva or Menelaus to change the picture, and Reset view to start again.
Look for the math

Two famous triangle facts look almost identical when written with lengths, yet one is about lines meeting and the other about dots lining up. This is the applet that puts them side by side: press one button or the other and drag the same triangle two different ways.

One product, two pictures

Let F lie on side AB, D on side BC and E on side AC (or on the extensions of those sides). Write the three length ratios in the order the applet's page uses. Ceva's theorem says the cevians AD, BE, CF meet at one point exactly when the product is 1. Menelaus' theorem says D, E, F lie on one straight line exactly when

AF/BF · BD/CD · CE/AE = 1

with the extra condition that one or all three of the dots sit on side extensions. That condition matters: a line cannot cut all three sides of a triangle inside it. The logic test checks the statement in both directions over a grid of 1,728 configurations and 3,935 random transversals, and it holds in every case with one or three outside dots.

Why the same number appears twice

By similar triangles, a line through A parallel to the transversal gives AF/BF = PD/BD and CE/AE = PD/CD, so the product is PD/BD · BD/CD · CD/PD = 1. Dropping perpendiculars instead gives the three ratios as AHa/BHb, BHb/CHc and CHc/AHa, which cancel in the same way.

With directed segments the two theorems separate cleanly: AF/FB · BD/DC · CE/EA is +1 for Ceva (no dots outside, or two) and −1 for Menelaus (one outside, or three). The unsigned formula above is the absolute value in both cases, which is why the little extra condition is needed. The test checks the signed form in 2,000 positions of each mode.

What the code copies from the applet

The original starts with A, B, C on a circle of radius one fifth of the shorter canvas side, rounded to whole pixels, and K at their centroid. Pressing Menelaus swaps A with F, limits E (the dot the applet calls K) to the line AC, and creates draggable dots D on BC and F on AB. After each drag the applet rebuilds just one other dot as a line intersection: move A and F is rebuilt, move B and D is rebuilt, move C and E is rebuilt, and dragging a side dot rebuilds the next one around the cycle.

That last detail is a quirk worth knowing about: moving a corner can leave one of the dots off the side it is supposed to lie on, while D, E, F stay in a line. The length product then need not be 1, because the page's premise no longer holds; drag D, E or F to put the dots back. The 29 logic checks follow this behaviour and also compare every move with a second transcription of the applet's own GeoSDoub.Intersect and DrawMenelaus instructions, including the NaN result for nearly parallel lines.

How this applet differs from its neighbours

The four applets around it ask different questions. MenelausBisector specialises both theorems to interior and exterior angle bisectors. MenelausFromCeva derives Menelaus from Ceva by multiplying six Ceva identities and taking a square root. MenelausProof shows two proofs of Menelaus alone. This applet is the side-by-side demonstration, with a switch between the concurrent cevians and the straight transversal; it makes no claim about bisectors or about which proof is best.

The applet's own page is Menelaus and Ceva Theorems at cut-the-knot.org, where the HTML really embeds CODE="Menelaus". The manifest name match points to Menelaus from 3D, a different page about Shutrick's three-dimensional proof: it has no Menelaus applet, so the live applet page and its linked explanation were used instead.

Try switching to Menelaus, dragging D, then dragging corner B: watch the bright line stay straight while the dot labelled D slides off its side until you drag it back.
